title: EvoLM: In Search of Lost Language Model Training Dynamics

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper makes mutually incompatible openness claims. The abstract says that only selected models, portions of datasets, and partial scripts will be released, because proprietary data and internal infrastructure prevent release of the full pipeline. Yet the Introduction claims the authors are “Open-sourcing 100+ LMs ... and their training data for all stages” and “Open-sourcing a comprehensive, transparent, and reproducible training pipeline and evaluation framework.” The latter claims materially overstate what the abstract says is available.

The text says that comparing “1B-320BT vs. 4B-80BT” as a fixed-compute comparison is misleading because it is “based solely on token counts” and ignores the higher FLOPs of the 4B model. But the selected token budgets are exactly the usual parameter-token compute normalization: 1B × 320B token-equivalents is approximately 4B × 80B token-equivalents. Exact FLOPs can differ by architecture, but the stated pairing does not ignore model size or parameter-update cost as claimed. The criticism contradicts the paper's own later description of this pair as being “under a fixed pre-training compute budget.”

Table 1 is repeatedly used as central evidence—for example, for claims that 1B-320BT outperforms 4B-80BT and for specific 4B-versus-1B post-training results—but no Table 1 appears anywhere in the supplied paper. Consequently, the numerical basis for these comparisons, including metrics, uncertainty, and the asserted compute matching, cannot be reviewed.

The paper calls the 8BT FineWeb + 42BT FineMath configuration a “modest replay budget (around 5%).” Table 2 gives 8BT replay out of 50BT total CPT tokens, which is 16%, not approximately 5% (and it is about 19% relative to the 42BT FineMath amount). This numerical misstatement is used to characterize the purported optimum and is repeated in Takeaway 3.

Takeaway 9 says RL saturation occurs at “4–8 epochs or 50–100K examples.” The preceding results text instead says greedy, Maj@16, and RM@16 “peak at around 8–16 epochs,” and that performance improves with RL data “up to around 150–200K examples.” Although Pass@16 may saturate earlier, the takeaway is framed as a general downstream-performance conclusion and contradicts the stated results for the other principal metrics.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sections 2.1–2.2 and Appendix B.2.3/B.3, SFT data and MATH/GSM8K-Platinum evaluation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The SFT corpus is explicitly said to aggregate data from GSM8K and MATH, while downstream evaluation includes GSM8K-Platinum (described as a revised version of the full GSM8K test set) and MATH. Appendix B.3.1 describes MATH as all 12,500 benchmark problems rather than identifying a held-out test split. The paper never specifies that benchmark test examples, near duplicates, or source problems were excluded from SFT, nor gives a deduplication protocol. This leaves direct train/test leakage unresolved and makes reported ID accuracy uninterpretable as held-out generalization.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2, ORM Score definition; claimed details in Appendix B.3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims that exact ORM normalization and calibration details, including scaling parameters, are in Appendix B.3. Appendix B.3 contains benchmark descriptions, a statement that Table 9 has standard errors, and examples, but no formula, calibration set identity/composition, fitted parameters, length-normalization method, reward-model prompt/template, or aggregation details. Since ORM is a major metric and the basis of Takeaway 12, this missing protocol prevents reproduction and validation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.4 and Appendix B.2.2, reinforcement-learning method
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says RL uses PPO and concludes that it uses “PPO with verifiable rewards,” but it never defines the training reward/verifier, answer extraction for rewards, reward scaling, treatment of invalid or truncated outputs, critic objective, or the source and construction of the RL dataset. Table 8 provides only a few optimizer and length hyperparameters. An external Skywork ORM is described for evaluation, not as the training reward. These omissions make the central RL experiments non-reproducible.

Appendix B.3.2 asserts that Table 9 reports standard errors for all main scaling results and that they were obtained from four random seeds. No Table 9 or any corresponding standard-error values are included. Thus the paper's claims about statistical uncertainty and multi-seed support are unsupported.

The methods state that models use the “LLaMA-2 [56] architecture,” but reference [56] is Touvron et al., “LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models” (the original LLaMA paper), not the Llama 2 technical report. The same reference is also the apparent basis for claims involving Llama 3.2 in Table 4. The cited source does not substantiate the version-specific architectural attribution.

Appendix B.2.3 cites FineMath as “FineMath [38],” but reference [38] is the FineWeb Datasets paper. Elsewhere, including Section 2.1, FineMath is cited as [2]. This is a concrete incorrect citation in the training-data documentation.

The text says the 1B and 4B models achieve “similar or slightly better results” than TinyLlama-1B and Qwen1.5-4B “across standard benchmarks.” Table 4 does not support this broad characterization: the 1B 320B-token model has lower average accuracy than TinyLlama (52.49 versus 53.23), and the 4B 320B-token model has lower average accuracy than Qwen1.5-4B (56.94 versus 58.86), while losing on most listed individual tasks. The immediately preceding caveat that tokenizers, schedules, data, and protocols are not harmonized further makes the competitive-performance framing unsuitable as evidence for a pretraining-diminishing-returns conclusion.

Section 2.1 says that for all configurations the authors analyze representative intermediate checkpoints to capture training dynamics and quantify trade-offs. Section 4.1 then demonstrates that intermediate checkpoints taken from longer runs systematically underperform dedicated shorter runs because they have different learning-rate trajectories, and explicitly warns that they are not valid surrogates for fully trained smaller models. The paper also states that Section 3 relies extensively on such checkpoints. Unless every Section 3 point is shown to be a separately completed training run, the scaling conclusions use a procedure the paper itself establishes as invalid; no per-result provenance is supplied.

The appendix says it shows three input-output examples, but the displayed material is a corrupted concatenation of different benchmarks and prompts. It begins under “GSM8KPlatinum” with a BoardgameQA-style animal-rule prompt, then inserts a CRUXEval function prompt and output, then a GSM8K vacation prompt and output, then resumes the initial animal-rule prompt and gives “True.” The example labels, inputs, and outputs do not correspond cleanly, so the claimed qualitative evidence cannot be interpreted or reproduced.
